title: Geng Handmade Never Left His Village, but Everyone Watching Him Is a City Person
dek: His builds need space and the freedom to make a mess — only possible in the countryside. City people are the ones who find them unusual. Like musicians who sing about the poor: the ones who actually buy in are city people, even intellectuals. The ads he embeds reach a city audience too.
why: This episode is slow and low-density; the first hour-plus is mostly village childhood and construction-site experience. The value is in the middle and back half: why a creator with enormous traffic won't take brand deals, and how he sees his own luck.
who: Creators doing content and building personal IPs, especially those with traffic but no monetization; and investors watching artisan commercialization and the short-video ecosystem.
skip: The childhood, migrant work and welding-school stretches can be fast-forwarded; starting from ‘money you can't handle’ is more useful.

points.h: A village influencer whose audience is entirely urban
points.body: Kuaishou has produced many rural influencers, some with tens of millions of followers, but their audiences are mostly rural, county-town or further down — big-city people can't get into them. Geng Handmade still hasn't left his village in Baoding, yet his audience is mainly urban. His own explanation: making things requires a lot of space and the willingness to make a mess, and those are only possible in the countryside; city people find it unusual. Luo Yonghao added an analogy: some original musicians who sing about the poor are loved precisely by city people, even intellectuals — the poor themselves don't care. The result: the ads embedded in his videos reach an entirely urban audience.

points.h: ‘Money you can't handle’ doesn't mean too much money
points.body: Geng Handmade once said he can't earn ‘money he can't handle’, which many fans read as ‘earning too much, can't handle it’. He clarified: it's not about the money, it's that his ability falls a bit short. Luo pressed: you're best at making content, your traffic is still astonishing, you could earn several times more by taking more brand deals — why not? Geng repeatedly said his ability isn't up to it. Brands usually come with a creative idea; he doesn't think much of their ideas, and can't come up with one he's satisfied with himself, so he just doesn't do it, preferring to post less. Luo had assumed it was laziness or a free spirit; after talking he found it was ‘can't get both sides to agree on a creative idea’.

points.h: Making is time-bounded, ideation is not
points.body: Geng broke down his own production process: purely by time, making takes longer than thinking up ideas. But the key is that making time is controllable, ideation time is not. When a brand deal comes, he'll spend three to five days, up to a month, on the idea; if he can't come up with one, he drops it. Some ideas took him two years and never came together; some came in a day. This explains why he posts so little — the bottleneck isn't capacity, it's ideas. He discusses ideas with his older and younger brothers, but in the end most of the ideas are his, and the others refine them. Now when he explains requirements to the team, they often don't understand; the requirements have gotten more complex than before.

points.h: No faking on camera, and it works in reality too
points.body: Luo asked him to his face: in all these years of videos, you've never cheated in the filming, right? Geng said he's never cheated on camera; if there were any, the requirement would be that the principle can also be shown in reality. Maybe there isn't enough time or enough parts swapped out, so it can't be that perfect, but basically it can be done. The joy of making things for him is that it really can be done, and then he films it — not filming something fake and being satisfied when everyone says it's good. This matches his understanding of ‘useful’: everything he wants to make is something that can actually be used and run in reality.

points.h: Filming upside-down hair washing, brother stands by with a sledgehammer
points.body: Luo asked whether there had been accidents during operations. Geng said rarely, but once: making the ram's horn required filling it with sand, baking it, then bending it slightly; while baking, the sand burst and flew into his brother's eye, and they rushed to the hospital — luckily the doctor said it was nothing serious. With the upside-down hair washing, he didn't realize the danger at first, thought washing hair upside down was perfectly logical, and only when he actually tried it found it terrifying — as soon as water covers your nose you panic, then you repeatedly adapt to water over your mouth, then turn. During filming he had his brother stand by with a sledgehammer, ready to smash the tub if something went wrong; that acrylic tub is actually very hard to smash, but having someone there made him feel safe. Whether his hair would get tangled, he hadn't considered at all.

points.h: He gives himself fifty percent luck
points.body: Luo has asked many guests the same question: how much of success is chance? Geng said chance is fairly large. His father said it outright: if you hadn't caught short video, hadn't caught this internet era, with your personality you'd never have succeeded. Geng's own review: if he really hadn't caught it, he might still be working a job, or doing farming or something else — ‘that outcome would be much worse than now’. He says both luck and effort are there, hard to tell which is bigger, but he gives himself ‘50% luck, 50% himself’. He doesn't believe he'd have made it in a different lane, with a different personality.

points.h: Daring to start a business because stainless steel doesn't depreciate
points.body: When he decided to go out on his own in '17, Geng's confidence came from a very practical judgment: stainless steel crafts keep for a long time, while labor costs keep rising, so if they don't sell now, they might sell later, and for more. It's not a tech product, it doesn't depreciate that fast — unlike hoarding a pile of pagers that won't move. So the worst case is losing his own labor, and the stuff doesn't rust sitting there. What he thought at the time was ‘at least there's no loss’, so he could give it a try. Even now he says he isn't very confident; his confidence back then only went as far as ‘worth a try’.

points.h: A super IP nobody has picked up
points.body: Some netizens suggested Geng Handmade do a national tour, and have Baoding's culture and tourism bureau develop it into a theme park: two hours' drive from Beijing, land isn't expensive, the works are ready-made — just set them out and put up a shed, and ticket revenue would cover the upkeep. Geng said he'd never thought about that direction, and culture-and-tourism officials had never talked to him about it. Luo repeatedly said what a waste, calling it a super IP. He also noted: these days computer CG and AI can make anything gorgeous, anything eerie; when you see enough eeriness in videos you stop finding it eerie, but walking through the workshop and touching each one, that's when it feels magical.
